facts.statement: The genus Globidentosuchus was first described in 2013 by T. M. Scheyer and colleagues.
facts.quote: Globidentosuchus was described in 2013 by T. M. Scheyer and colleagues

facts.statement: The only known species within the genus is Globidentosuchus brachyrostris.
facts.quote: the type and only species being G. brachyrostris

facts.statement: Fossils of Globidentosuchus are found in the Middle and Upper Members of the Urumaco Formation in Urumaco, Venezuela, dating to the late Middle to Late Miocene.
facts.quote: known from the late Middle to Late Miocene of the Middle and the Upper Members of the Urumaco Formation at Urumaco, Venezuela

facts.statement: Globidentosuchus had a very short, robust skull equipped with spherical teeth adapted for crushing mollusc shells.
facts.quote: Its skull was very short and robust, with large units of spherical teeth used to break the shells of molluscs as part of its durophagus diet

facts.statement: Globidentosuchus was a small species measuring approximately 1.72 meters in length and weighing about 16.7 kilograms.
facts.quote: Globidentosuchus was a small caimanine species at only 1.72 m meters in length and 16.7 kg in weight

facts.statement: Each lower jaw of Globidentosuchus contained 18 teeth, consisting of 10 conical front teeth and 8 spherical, robust rear teeth.
facts.quote: Each mandible preserves 18 teeth, 10 conical teeth in the anterior portion and 8 spherical, robust teeth in the posterior portion

facts.statement: The tightly packed spherical teeth formed a specialized crushing unit designed to break hard-shelled prey like molluscs.
facts.quote: These spherical teeth were tightly packed, making a crushing unit that was built to crush molluscs

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses often place Globidentosuchus as one of the most basal members of the Caimaninae subfamily.
facts.quote: Globidentosuchus is often recovered as one of or the most basal caimanines

facts.statement: It is debated whether Globidentosuchus represents a relict population of basal caimanines that survived in Central and northern South America into the Late Miocene, a hypothesis requiring more fossil evidence to confirm.
facts.quote: Hastings et al. (2013) proposed that this phylogenetic position is because of a potential relict population of basal caimanines that persisted in Central America and/or northern South America into the Late Miocene, as shown by Globidentosuchus and its basal relatives Gnatusuchus and Culebrasuchus, though more fossils are needed to confirm this

facts.statement: Globidentosuchus lived between 11.63 and 5.333 million years ago during the Tortonian to Messinian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Tortonian to Messinian (11.63 to 5.333 million years ago)

facts.statement: Globidentosuchus inhabited the wetlands of northern Venezuela until the Late Miocene, going extinct by the Early Pliocene.
facts.quote: Globidentosuchus inhabited the wetlands of the northern Urumaco Formation in Venezuela into the Late Miocene before eventually dying out by the Early Pliocene

facts.statement: Globidentosuchus shared its Late Miocene wetland habitat with giant crocodilians such as Purussaurus, Mourasuchus, and Gryposuchus.
facts.quote: Some of the enormous crocodilians that coexisted with Globidentosuchus included the enormous caimain Purussaurus, the bizarre Mourasuchus and large-bodied gharials of the genus Gryposuchus
